lesson.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
lesson.subtitle: groot → groter → grootst; goed → beter → best

hook.title: More, Most — and the Irregulars
hook.content: Dutch adds -er and -st: groot → groter → grootst. The high-frequency irregulars are the same ones English has: goed → beter → best, veel → meer → meest.

pattern.title: -er compares, -st crowns
pattern.content: Groter dan ('bigger than'), het grootst ('the biggest'). Use dan for 'than' and als for 'as': even groot als. The adjective still takes -e when the phrase is definite.
pattern.linguist_note: The comparative -er and superlative -st are shared Germanic endings; the suppletion goed/beter/best mirrors good/better/best.
pattern.trap_note: Do not say groter als for 'bigger than'. Dan compares, als equates.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Comparatives & Superlatives):
exercises.target_answer: groot, klein, goed, beter, best, dan
exercises.meaning: big, great, small, good, better, best, than; then
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Comparatives & Superlatives": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The house is bigger than the book.”?
options: Het huis is groter dan het boek.
Het huis is groter als het boek.
Het huis is meer groot dan het boek.
exercises.target_answer: Het huis is groter dan het boek.
exercises.meaning: The house is bigger than the book.
exercises.explanation: “Het huis is groter dan het boek.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Comparatives & Superlatives”.

exercises.idea: My house is big, your house is bigger.
cues: It means: My house is big, your house is bigger.
idea_parts: My house is big, your house is bigger.
exercises.target_answer: Mijn huis is groot, jouw huis is groter.
exercises.meaning: My house is big, your house is bigger.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn huis is groot, jouw huis is groter.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — -er compares, -st crowns.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not say groter als for 'bigger than'. Dan compares, als equates.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.german: Dit boek is beter dan dat boek.
exercises.natural: This book is better than that book.
options: This book is better than that book.
not This book is better than that book.
This book is better than that book. (1)
exercises.target_answer: This book is better than that book.
exercises.meaning: This book is better than that book.
exercises.explanation: “Dit boek is beter dan dat boek.” is word-for-word “This book is better than that book.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: -er compares, -st crowns.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: She is the best.
exercises.explanation: “Zij is de beste.” reuses only material taught in “Comparatives & Superlatives” — -er compares, -st crowns.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Zij is de beste.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising -er compares, -st crowns.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The train is faster than the bike.”
twist.target_answer: De trein is sneller dan de fiets.
twist.explanation: Snel → sneller → snelst; dan marks the comparison.

summary.outcome: Compare with -er/-st, dan and als, including the irregular goed/beter/best.
summary.takeaway: Comparison is one ending plus two tiny words: dan for than, als for as.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Comparison Gym.

groot.etymology_derivation: English great and Dutch groot are the same word.

klein.etymology_derivation: English clean once meant 'small, fine'; Dutch kept klein for small.

goed.etymology_derivation: English good and Dutch goed are the same word.

beter.etymology_derivation: The irregular comparative of goed, like English better from good.

best.etymology_derivation: The irregular superlative of goed, like English best.

dan.context_phrase: Het huis is groter dan het boek.
dan.context_translation: The house is bigger than the book.
dan.etymology_derivation: English than and then are the same root; Dutch dan covers both.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.

f_v.name: The F → V Bridge
f_v.phonetic_rule: English f often corresponds to Dutch v: father → vader, foot → voet, fish → vis.
f_v.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic f to v in many positions; English kept the voiceless consonant.
f_v.philological_note: Northern Dutch often devoices v to [f], especially in vr-/vl- clusters and word-finally; the spelling keeps the historical v.

s_z.name: The S → Z Bridge
s_z.phonetic_rule: English s often corresponds to Dutch z: sun → zon, sea → zee, salt → zout.
s_z.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic s before vowels; English kept s.
s_z.philological_note: Clusters sn/sm/sl keep s (sneeuw, smal, slapen); loans such as school and straat also keep s.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.

vowel_ui.name: The UI Bridge
vowel_ui.phonetic_rule: Dutch ui is /œy/ and often answers to English ou/ow: house → huis, mouse → muis, out → uit.
vowel_ui.historical_linguistics: Dutch ui spells a front rounded diphthong with no close English equivalent; the English spelling twin is a memory hook.
vowel_ui.philological_note: Do not pronounce ui as two English beats; it is one gliding vowel.

vowel_oe.name: The OE Bridge
vowel_oe.phonetic_rule: Dutch oe is /u/ and often answers to English oo/u in spelling: book → boek, foot → voet, good → goed.
vowel_oe.historical_linguistics: The Dutch digraph oe spells a long /u/; English oo spells several different vowels, so this is a spelling/cognacy bridge.
vowel_oe.philological_note: Dutch oe is /u/, not the /ʊ/ of English book. Read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.
